lead: A second order linear ODE needs two solutions before you can write its general solution. Not any two: they must be genuinely different, not one a constant multiple of the other. The Wronskian is one determinant that answers this yes-or-no question, and Abel's formula makes the answer cheap — check it at a single point of the interval. Every exam question that asks for a general solution, and every solver that builds one, rests on this test.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for how y = e^(mx) produces solutions, and 2×2 determinants from school algebra.

blocks.text: Take functions y₁, y₂, …, y_n defined on an interval I. They are linearly dependent on I if you can find constants c₁, c₂, …, c_n, not all zero, such that c₁y₁ + c₂y₂ + … + c_n y_n = 0 for every x in I. If the only choice is c₁ = c₂ = … = c_n = 0, the functions are linearly independent on I.
The phrase 'for every x in I' carries the whole definition. Two functions may agree at one point and still be independent; dependence is a statement about the entire interval.
Example. y₁ = x and y₂ = 3x are dependent on any interval, because 3·x − 1·(3x) = 0 everywhere. y₁ = eˣ and y₂ = e²ˣ are independent: c₁eˣ + c₂e²ˣ = 0 for all x forces c₁ = c₂ = 0.

Superposition makes this the right question. If y₁ and y₂ solve a homogeneous linear ODE, so does every combination c₁y₁ + c₂y₂. The solutions form a vector space, and independence counts its dimension. A second order linear homogeneous ODE has a two-dimensional solution space; an nth order one has dimension n. So n independent solutions are exactly enough to describe every solution.
Build a table. Row 1 holds the functions, row 2 their first derivatives, row 3 their second derivatives, up to derivative n−1. The Wronskian W(y₁, …, y_n) is the determinant of that n×n table.

blocks.where: y₁ and y₂ are the two functions on I, and the prime means d/dx.

blocks.text: For three functions the table is three rows deep: rows y, y′, y″. The determinant of that 3×3 table is W.

The test. If W(x₀) ≠ 0 at even one point x₀ of I, the functions are linearly independent on I. Reason: suppose c₁y₁ + c₂y₂ = 0. Differentiate to get c₁y₁′ + c₂y₂′ = 0. At x₀ these are two linear equations in c₁ and c₂ whose determinant is W(x₀). A nonzero determinant forces c₁ = c₂ = 0.

Warning. The reverse fails for arbitrary functions. On (−1, 1) take y₁ = x² and y₂ = x|x|. They are independent, yet W = 0 at every point. So W = 0 alone does not prove dependence in general. For solutions of a linear ODE the story is cleaner — that is the next section.
Write the second order equation as y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = 0, with P and Q continuous on I. Abel's formula says W(x) = W₀ exp(−∫P dx), where W₀ = W(x₀) and the integral runs from x₀ to x.
Quick derivation: W′ = y₁y₂″ − y₁″y₂. Replace each y″ by −Py′ − Qy. The Q terms cancel, leaving W′ = −P W, a first order separable equation whose solution is the formula.

Consequence: exp is never zero, so W is either zero at every point of I or at no point. Checking one value settles the whole interval. For an nth order equation the same formula holds with P the coefficient of y^(n−1), after dividing by the leading coefficient.

Fundamental set. Any n solutions of an nth order linear homogeneous ODE with W ≠ 0 form a fundamental set. Every solution is y = c₁y₁ + … + c_n y_n, the general solution. Given n initial conditions y(x₀), y′(x₀), …, y^(n−1)(x₀), the constants solve a linear system whose determinant is W(x₀) ≠ 0, so they are unique. With variable coefficients, see Chapter 2.8 for how one known solution produces the second.

figure.caption: The first row holds the two solutions and the second row their derivatives; the determinant of this table is W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂, and one nonzero value proves independence.

spec.title: Wronskian of two solutions
spec.aria: A two-row table holding the two solutions in the first row and their derivatives in the second, whose determinant is the Wronskian.

examples.question: For y₁ = eˣ and y₂ = e²ˣ, form the Wronskian. Evaluate it at x = 0 and x = 1 and decide whether the pair is independent. Then repeat for y₁ = x and y₂ = 3x.
steps: Set up the determinant: W = |y₁ y₂; y₁′ y₂′| = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂.
Substitute: W = eˣ(2e²ˣ) − eˣ(e²ˣ) = 2e³ˣ − e³ˣ = e³ˣ.
At x = 0: W = e⁰ = 1. Nonzero, so eˣ and e²ˣ are linearly independent on every interval.
At x = 1: W = e³ ≈ 20.0855. Also nonzero, the same conclusion.
Second pair: y₁′ = 1 and y₂′ = 3, so W = x·3 − 1·3x = 0 for every x. The pair is dependent, since 3·x + (−1)·3x = 0.
examples.answer: W = e³ˣ ≠ 0 for the exponential pair, so it is independent; W = 0 for x and 3x, so that pair is dependent.

traps: Reading W = 0 at one point as dependence. For solutions of a linear ODE this is safe because W is zero everywhere or nowhere; for arbitrary functions it is false, as x² and x|x| show.

Writing W = y₁′y₂ − y₁y₂′ and then using W = W₀exp(−∫P dx). Both orders appear in textbooks. This book fixes W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂, so keep that choice in every step. A sign flip changes the sign of W but not whether W is zero, so independence verdicts are unchanged — just stay consistent.
Using the coefficient of y″ instead of y′ in Abel's formula. Divide the ODE by its leading coefficient first.
Judging independence by appearance. cos 2x and 2cos²x − 1 look different but are the same function; only the determinant decides.
Giving only two rows for three functions. The Wronskian of y₁, y₂, y₃ needs rows y, y′, y″.

quiz.q: State what it means for functions y₁, …, y_n to be linearly dependent on an interval I.
quiz.a: Constants c₁, …, c_n, not all zero, with c₁y₁ + … + c_n y_n = 0 for every x in I.

quiz.q: Write the Wronskian of two functions y₁ and y₂.
Why does a nonzero Wronskian at a single point prove independence?
quiz.a: Dependence gives c₁y₁ + c₂y₂ = 0; differentiate and set x = x₀. The two equations in c₁, c₂ have determinant W(x₀) ≠ 0, so c₁ = c₂ = 0.

quiz.q: Compute W for y₁ = e^(2x) and y₂ = e^(−2x).
Compute W for y₁ = sin x and y₂ = cos x.
quiz.a: W = sin x(−sin x) − cos x(cos x) = −sin²x − cos²x = −1; nonzero.

quiz.q: On (−1, 1), y₁ = x² and y₂ = x|x| have W = 0 everywhere yet are independent. Why does this not contradict the Wronskian test?
quiz.a: Nonzero W implies independence, but zero W implies dependence only for solutions of a linear ODE. x² and x|x| are not such a pair on that interval.

quiz.q: For y″ − 4y = 0, W(0) = 5. Find W(x) and decide whether any solution pair can have W(x) = 0 at x = 2.
quiz.a: P = 0, so W(x) = 5 for all x by Abel's formula; it is never zero at x = 2.

quiz.q: Why do n initial conditions determine the constants in the general solution uniquely?
quiz.a: They give n linear equations in c₁, …, c_n whose coefficient determinant is W(x₀) ≠ 0, so the solution is unique.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same determinant becomes the fundamental matrix in systems of ODEs, and its determinant is the Wronskian of the system. Sturm-Liouville theory in Unit 3 uses W to prove that eigenfunctions belonging to different eigenvalues are orthogonal. In control engineering, a related Gramian decides whether a system can be steered to any state. Search 'Abel identity Wronskian' and 'fundamental matrix solution'.
